title: All the microbes you can’t have - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A 1986 White House decision to regulate engineered microbes under the 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), using a scientifically arbitrary 'cross-genus DNA' trigger, has frozen commercialization of plastic-eating, metal-leaching, and pollution-sensing microbes for forty years; companies that route around TSCA via gene-shuffling or FDA/cosmetic classification have commercialized products, while Brazil and Israel show that fast, workable engineered-organism approval regimes are achievable without US-style paralysis.

themes.theme: How TSCA came to govern biology

insights.claim: In 1983, biotech company AGS applied to field-test a genetically modified 'ice-minus' microbe (with a single gene deleted) sprayed on crops to prevent frost damage, triggering the first US legal fight over releasing engineered organisms into the environment.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Marks the origin point of the regulatory regime that, per this article, still blocks most engineered-microbe commercialization forty years later.
insights.locator: opening paragraph, 'In 1983, a biochemical company called AGS'

insights.claim: Activist Jeremy Rifkin sued to block AGS's field trials, arguing the NIH had skipped a required Environmental Impact Statement and that the modified microbes could escape and affect rainfall; activists later cut through a fence and uprooted about 2,000 of 2,400 test strawberry plants after AGS won the right to proceed in 1987.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Illustrates how activist legal and direct action, not scientific risk data, was the proximate trigger for the regulatory framework still governing engineered microbes today.
insights.locator: 'But an activist named Jeremy Rifkin then sued'

insights.claim: After the Rifkin lawsuit, White House staff, EPA, and USDA lawyers concluded no new law was needed: the 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), written for industrial chemicals, would apply to engineered microbes because genomes are made of chemicals.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The entire modern US engineered-microbe regulatory bottleneck traces to a single administrative interpretive choice in the 1980s, not a purpose-built biosafety law — meaning it is fixable by an equally administrative decision (an EPA memo) rather than new legislation.
insights.locator: 'They concluded that no new laws were needed'

insights.claim: Between 1987 and 2018, researchers filed more than 240 applications to develop TSCA-covered engineered microbes, and only a few were ever approved for widespread use.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A sub-single-digit-percent approval rate over three decades is a quantifiable measure of how completely TSCA has frozen this category of biotech commercialization — useful as a baseline for judging any future reform's impact.
insights.locator: 'The TSCA is a regulatory black hole'

insights.claim: Under a 1997 EPA rule implementing TSCA, combining DNA from species across different genera automatically triggers full regulatory review, regardless of whether the resulting organism is demonstrably safe.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The bright-line 'cross-genus' test, not actual risk assessment, is the mechanical gate that determines whether a microbial biotech product can ever reach market in the US.
insights.locator: 'Under a 1997 EPA rule'

themes.theme: Technologies stuck in the TSCA black hole

insights.claim: University of Texas at Austin engineers created FAST-PETase, a computationally-optimized enzyme 98% identical to a naturally evolved PET-plastic-degrading enzyme found near a Japanese recycling plant, that digests PET plastic bottles in under 24 hours versus six weeks for the natural version — but placing the enzyme's gene back into its original host microbe still triggers TSCA and blocks its use.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A dramatically faster (weeks-to-hours) plastics recycling solution already exists technically but is legally blocked from deployment on landfills, representing a concrete, quantifiable opportunity cost of the current regulatory regime.
insights.locator: 'Engineers at the University of Texas at Austin therefore took'

insights.claim: Researchers have engineered E. coli that can detect heavy metals in water at very low concentrations — as little as five parts per billion of cadmium, and in a 2010 Chinese study, seven nanomolar mercury (seven times below the EPA's own contamination threshold) — but none of these biosensor strains can be used outside the lab because they contain intergeneric DNA that triggers TSCA.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Cheap, highly sensitive biosensors that could undercut existing water-testing methods and beat EPA's own detection thresholds are commercially blocked purely on classification grounds, not performance or safety grounds.
insights.locator: 'Researchers have already created E. coli'

insights.claim: The US has enough active mines to meet all domestic mineral needs if it could capture 90 percent of the byproduct metals currently discarded during ore purification, but conventional recovery is energy-intensive and chemically toxic, while microbial bioleaching offers a cleaner, self-powering alternative that remains regulatorily constrained.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Bioleaching-enabled byproduct capture is framed as a potential path to US mineral self-sufficiency without new mines, relevant to critical-minerals and reshoring narratives, but is currently bottlenecked by the same TSCA regime.
insights.locator: 'Mining is another missed opportunity'

insights.claim: Cornell researchers in a 2021 study identified 89 genes involved in acid production by Gluconobacter oxydans B58 and, by deleting some and overexpressing others, created a variant that extracts rare earth metals 73 percent faster than the ordinary microbe — but even this within-species edit is complicated by TSCA because the marker gene used to select engineered cells typically comes from another organism.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Even a 73% efficiency gain in rare-earth extraction — directly relevant to critical minerals supply chains — is caught by TSCA's cross-genus trigger via a technical side-effect (antibiotic marker genes) of standard genetic engineering methods.
insights.locator: 'In a 2021 study, Cornell researchers found'

themes.theme: The opacity and severity of EPA's process

insights.claim: The EPA issues one of three verdicts on engineered-microbe applications under TSCA: 'no unreasonable risk' (allowed after a 90-day wait), 'unreasonable risk' (fully blocked), or a Section 5(e) consent order, which the article describes as 'indefinite regulatory purgatory' that caps production volumes and can mandate incineration of every soil sample or surface the microbe touched.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The consent-order outcome functions as a de facto ban with extreme compliance costs (mandated incineration of contaminated materials), making it a critical risk factor for any company planning to commercialize an engineered microbe in the US.
insights.locator: 'The consent order is meant for cases where the agency can't rule out risk'

insights.claim: Unlike its treatment of chemicals, where TSCA requires the EPA to make application details public, the EPA keeps engineered-microbe applications private, so people near proposed release sites cannot learn what organisms are being tested, and companies cannot learn from prior applicants' EPA feedback.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Application secrecy compounds the regulatory bottleneck by forcing every company to re-discover EPA's unwritten requirements from scratch, wasting capital industry-wide — an argument for the article's proposed fix of releasing historical case files.
insights.locator: 'When used to regulate chemicals, the TSCA obliges'

insights.claim: The EPA has never published a checklist of requirements for engineered-microbe applications, so companies must submit applications based on guesses about what the agency wants to know.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Lack of published criteria is itself an entry barrier that likely favors larger, better-capitalized incumbents who can afford repeated rounds of guess-and-check with the EPA over smaller biotech startups.
insights.locator: 'Companies do not always know why the EPA rejects'

insights.claim: Only a handful of engineered microbes have ever been approved for commercial use under TSCA, including one in 1997 approved for limited use as a nitrogen-fixing biofertilizer in alfalfa.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A near-40-year track record of essentially no new approvals is a strong prior against betting on near-term commercialization of any new engineered microbe that requires standard TSCA review.
insights.locator: 'Only a few have ever been approved for commercial use'

insights.claim: Pivot Bio sells nitrogen-fixing microbes that colonize plant roots and, the company says, can replace about a quarter of the synthetic fertilizer farmers normally use without hurting crop yields; in 2022 alone its microbes reportedly replaced an estimated 32,000 tons of synthetic fertilizer across millions of acres.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Pivot Bio is a live commercial-scale case study of successfully navigating around TSCA at real agricultural scale (millions of acres), making it a reference point for what a TSCA-compliant biotech business model looks like today.
insights.locator: 'Pivot Bio, for example, sells genetically engineered microbes'

insights.claim: Pivot Bio avoided triggering TSCA by reshuffling genes within a single organism rather than importing DNA across species lines, but this workaround is not generalizable: for tasks like plastic degradation or metal leaching, the needed genes often don't exist in any single organism that is both easy to engineer and hardy enough to survive in the field.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The gene-shuffling workaround only works for a narrow subset of applications, meaning most higher-value engineered-microbe use cases (plastics, mining, biosensing) remain structurally blocked even as some agricultural applications succeed.
insights.locator: 'Pivot dodged TSCA by reshuffling genes'

insights.claim: Microbes classified as pesticides, agricultural products, or ingestible therapeutics are reviewed by the EPA's biopesticide office, USDA's APHIS, or the FDA respectively instead of under general TSCA review, letting products in those categories reach the environment via runoff, sewage, and toilets while avoiding the TSCA bottleneck entirely.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Regulatory arbitrage by product classification (biopesticide vs. TSCA-covered microbe) is a viable strategic lever for biotech companies choosing how to position and file a new engineered-organism product.
insights.locator: 'Some engineered microbes have avoided the black hole of TSCA'

insights.claim: ZBiotics engineered a Bacillus subtilis strain that breaks down acetaldehyde (the toxic byproduct of alcohol metabolism) and sold it as a pre-drinking probiotic, avoiding FDA pre-market approval entirely by showing B. subtilis is 'Generally Recognized as Safe' rather than going through TSCA.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a specific, replicable regulatory path (GRAS self-affirmation for a probiotic/dietary supplement) that let a consumer engineered-microbe product reach market quickly despite containing intergeneric DNA.
insights.locator: 'A company called ZBiotics has engineered a strain'

insights.claim: Lantern Bioworks sold an engineered Streptococcus mutans variant designed to permanently colonize the mouth, outcompete cavity-causing natural S. mutans, and prevent cavities, by marketing it as a cosmetic rather than a drug to avoid FDA's rigorous drug-approval process — despite long-term effects on the oral microbiome and person-to-person transmissibility (e.g. via kissing) being unknown.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Illustrates the flip side of regulatory arbitrage: a permanently colonizing engineered organism with unknown transmissibility and long-term effects reaching consumers via a lighter-touch 'cosmetic' classification, a genuine biosafety gap the article itself flags as a risk.
insights.locator: 'Another company, Lantern Bioworks, sold an engineered microbe'

themes.theme: Why the genus-based science doesn't hold up

insights.claim: The 1980s decision to regulate engineered microbes under TSCA assumed cross-genus gene transfers were rare in nature and therefore warranted special scrutiny, but a study of 93,000 microbial genomes found cross-genus DNA swaps occur naturally in roughly a third of them.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: This is the article's core scientific rebuttal of TSCA's regulatory logic: the foundational premise (cross-genus transfer is unnatural/rare) is empirically false, undermining the legitimacy of the entire 40-year framework.
insights.locator: 'One study of 93,000 microbial genomes'

insights.claim: Genera are human-constructed taxonomic categories rather than fixed biological facts, and taxonomists periodically reclassify species — in 2020, hundreds of species in the Lactobacillus genus (common in probiotics and fermented foods) were reclassified, meaning gene swaps that would not have triggered TSCA before 2020 would trigger it today for the same biological material.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Shows the TSCA trigger can flip on or off for identical biology purely due to unrelated taxonomic reclassification, exposing the rule as arbitrary rather than risk-based — a strong argument for regulatory reform advocates.
insights.locator: 'In 2020, researchers reclassified hundreds of microbial species'

insights.claim: Four decades of field trial data now show engineered microbes released into the environment mostly die off quickly because they are outcompeted by native organisms adapted to that environment — a lab-derived E. coli population dropped 100,000-fold in soil within eight days.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Empirical persistence data now exists to replace the speculative 1980s risk assumptions, providing an evidence base for a risk-tiered rather than blanket TSCA approach.
insights.locator: 'A population of E. coli from the laboratory'

insights.claim: Some risks are real and persistent: an engineered phenol-eating microbe released by Estonian researchers in the 1980s left traces of its inserted gene detectable in the soil decades later, and some root-colonizing engineered microbes persist in soil for decades.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The article balances its deregulation argument by acknowledging genuine long-term persistence risk exists in some cases, arguing for calibrated data-driven standards rather than wholesale deregulation.
insights.locator: 'An engineered phenol-eating microbe released by Estonian researchers'

insights.claim: The EPA applies TSCA inconsistently across categories: researchers running a small-scale experiment with a new chemical can get a Congressionally-legislated exemption from EPA review, but the EPA revokes that same exemption when researchers want to run an equivalent small-scale experiment with an engineered microbe.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the EPA holds engineered biology to a stricter standard than industrial chemicals under the very same statute, a specific inconsistency reformers could target without needing new legislation.
insights.locator: 'The EPA does not even apply TSCA consistently'

insights.claim: Because Congress never explicitly codified TSCA's application to biology, the EPA administrator could reform the framework unilaterally by memo — clarifying evaluation criteria and releasing three decades of case files — without requiring new legislation.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Identifies a low-friction, executive-branch-only reform path (an EPA memo) that could unlock the stalled pipeline of plastic-eating, metal-leaching, and biosensing microbes without waiting on Congress.
insights.locator: 'The TSCA could change tomorrow'

insights.claim: Congress's authority for the EPA to collect TSCA user fees from chemical companies, granted in 2016, expires midway through 2026, creating a legislative vehicle to which broader engineered-microbe reforms could be attached.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A concrete 2026 legislative deadline (the user-fee reauthorization) is a specific catalyst window to watch for possible TSCA reform riders relevant to biotech investors and policymakers.
insights.locator: 'In 2016, Congress authorized the EPA'

insights.claim: Brazil approved the first unconstrained environmental release of an engineered organism — a genetically modified Aedes aegypti mosquito whose modified males cause their offspring to die at the larval stage — and in Brazilian cities where released, wild mosquito populations have dropped 80 to 96 percent.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Brazil's approach shows a working regulatory model that has already delivered large, measurable public-health results (80-96% mosquito population reduction), serving as evidence that faster approval need not mean unsafe outcomes.
insights.locator: 'Brazil approved the first unconstrained, environmental release'

insights.claim: Israel's approval process for releasing engineered microbes routes applications to a panel of government representatives and academics led by the Ministry of Agriculture, which typically renders a yes/no decision within a few months — in 2017, researchers received approval to release explosive-sensing engineered microbes in the Israeli desert in under a year.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Israel's few-months review timeline versus the US's decades-long near-total freeze is a stark comparative benchmark for how much faster engineered-microbe commercialization could move under a differently designed regulatory process.
insights.locator: 'Israel is even more efficient with its approval process'

insights.claim: The article concludes the US does not need to adopt a system as permissive as Israel's, but does need regulation that biotechnologists can actually navigate — arguing reform should mean clear data and field-trial standards, not throwing open the door to any engineered microbe.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Frames the reform ask as targeted process fixes (clear standards, published criteria, use of accumulated field data) rather than deregulation, which is the more politically viable framing for policymakers to act on.
insights.quote: It's why plastic-eating and mine-seeking microbes, for all their promise, have never left the lab.
insights.locator: closing paragraph
